content: Elytrigia repens, commonly known as Couch Grass, is a widespread grass species native to most regions of Europe, Asia, and northwest Africa. It is also referred to by other names such as twitch, quick grass, quitch grass, dog grass, and quackgrass. This grass is characterized by its creeping rhizomes, which allow it to spread rapidly across grasslands. The flower spike measures between 10 and 30 cm in length, with spikelets that are 1–2 cm long, 5–7 mm wide, and 3 mm thick, containing three to eight florets. The glumes are typically 7–12 mm long and are usually awnless or have only a short awn. There are three recognized subspecies of Elytrigia repens, one of which includes an additional variety: Elytrigia repens subsp. repens: Found throughout most of the species' range. Elytrigia repens subsp. repens var. repens: Awns are usually absent or, if present, very short. Elytrigia repens subsp. repens var. Sell.: Awns are present and can grow up to 15 mm in length. Elytrigia repens subsp. elongatiformis (Drobow) Tzvelev: Found in central and southwestern Asia, as well as far southeastern Europe (e.g., Ukraine). Elytrigia repens subsp. longearistata N.R. Cui: Found in western China (Xinjiang). Hybrids of Elytrigia repens have been documented with several related grass species, including Elytrigia juncea (Elytrigia × laxa), Elytrigia atherica (Elytrigia × drucei), and the barley species Hordeum secalinum (× Elytrordeum langei). Ecology The foliage of Couch Grass serves as an important forage source for many grazing mammals. Its seeds are consumed by various grassland bird species, particularly buntings and finches. Additionally, it is a host plant for certain butterfly species, such as the Essex Skipper (Thymelicus lineola). Cultivation and Uses Couch Grass has become naturalized in many parts of the world and is often classified as an invasive weed. It is notoriously difficult to eradicate from garden environments. One effective method of removal involves digging deeply into the soil to extract as much of the grass as possible, followed by covering the area with a thick layer of woodchips. To further inhibit regrowth, cardboard can be placed beneath the woodchips. The long, white rhizomes of the grass will dry out and die if left exposed on the surface. Medical Use Couch Grass has been utilized in herbal medicine since the Classical Greek period. It is known that sick dogs instinctively dig up and consume the roots of this plant. In medieval times, herbalists used Couch Grass to treat conditions such as inflamed bladders, painful urination, and water retention. The plant also possesses antiseptic properties.
